questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following marked structures does not form part of the laryngeal skeleton?
questions.explanation:
The structure marked A is the hyoid bone, which is not part of the laryngeal skeleton. The marked structures are hyoid bone, thyroid cartilage, epiglottis, and cricoid cartilage.

The laryngeal skeleton is formed by cartilages connected by ligaments and fibrous membranes. Thyroid, cricoid, and most of the arytenoid cartilages are hyaline. Corniculate, cuneiform, triticeal, epiglottic cartilages and the apices of the arytenoids are elastic.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following laryngeal cartilages is not paired?
questions.explanation: Cricoid is an unpaired laryngeal cartilage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following cartilages forms a complete ring?
questions.explanation:
Cricoid cartilage forms a complete ring around the airway and is the only laryngeal cartilage to do so.

Clinical significance: in Sellick manoeuvre, cricoid pressure is applied to occlude the esophagus without occluding the airway, helping prevent regurgitation of gastric contents during rapid induction. The cricoid is also the narrowest part of the pediatric airway.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: All of the following ligaments are components of the external laryngeal membrane except:
questions.explanation:
The cricothyroid ligament/membrane is an intrinsic laryngeal membrane rather than an external laryngeal membrane.

The cricothyroid ligament lies between the cricoid and thyroid cartilages and has right and left lateral parts (conus elasticus) and a thickened median or anterior cricothyroid ligament.

Extrinsic ligaments and membranes include the thyrohyoid membrane, hyoepiglottic ligament, and cricotracheal ligament. Intrinsic membranes include the quadrangular membrane, cricothyroid membrane, and thyroepiglottic ligament.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statement is true regarding the laryngeal cavity?

options.text: Laryngeal ventricle is between laryngeal inlet and vestibular folds
Vocal cords are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Rima glottidis is present between the vocal folds
Ventricle is a pouch from the anterior end of the saccule

questions.correctAnswerText: Rima glottidis is present between the vocal folds
questions.explanation:
Rima glottidis is the aperture between the vocal folds.

The upper laryngeal cavity extends from the laryngeal inlet to the vestibular folds; the vestibule lies between these. The middle part extends from rima vestibuli to rima glottidis. The ventricle lies between the vestibular and vocal folds, while the saccule is a pouch from the anterior end of the ventricle. The lower or infraglottic cavity extends from the vocal cords to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.

The larynx is generally lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, except the vocal folds, lingual surface of the epiglottis, and upper part of the aryepiglottic folds, which are lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A trumpet player presented with hoarseness of voice, cough, and a reducible neck swelling. The neck swelling increases in size on performing the Valsalva maneuver. Which of the following regions would you expect to find a defect in?
questions.explanation:
The scenario is suggestive of a laryngocele. The defect is in the saccule, represented by region A in the source diagram. The other labelled structures are B: ventricle, C: vestibular ligament, and D: vocal ligament.

The saccule ascends forward from the anterior end of the ventricle between the vestibular fold and thyroid cartilage. It is conical and contains many mucous glands whose secretions lubricate the vocal cords.

Laryngocele is an air-filled cystic swelling caused by dilatation of the saccule and is associated with activities that raise transglottic pressure, such as trumpet playing, glass blowing, or weight lifting. It may be internal, external, or combined. External laryngocele presents as a reducible neck swelling that enlarges with coughing or Valsalva.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: You are an ENT resident consulting on a famous metal singer, who presented with complaints of hoarseness of voice. You perform laryngoscopy and ask him to phonate. You notice that he is using his false vocal cords to generate a classic 'death growl'. Which of the following structures form the ligament enclosed in these vocal cords?

options.text: Upper free margin of cricothyroid ligament
Lower free margin of quadrangular membrane
Upper free margin of quadrangular membrane
Upper free margin of conus elasticus

questions.correctAnswerText: Lower free margin of quadrangular membrane
questions.explanation:
The vestibular ligament is enclosed within the false vocal cords. The lower free margin of the quadrangular membrane is thickened to form the vestibular ligament.

False vocal cords are formed by vestibular folds and contain the vestibular ligament, a few fibres of thyroarytenoideus, and mucous glands. True vocal cords extend from the thyroid angle to the vocal processes of the arytenoids and contain the vocal ligament and subepithelial connective tissue. The upper free margin of the cricovocal ligament/cricothyroid membrane/conus elasticus is thickened to form the vocal ligament.

The vestibular ligament is enclosed within the false vocal cords. The lower free margin of the quadrangular membrane is thickened to form the vestibular ligament.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient with bronchogenic carcinoma presents to your OPD complaining of hoarseness of voice. On laryngoscopy, you ask him to phonate and notice that the left vocal cord does not abduct. Which of the following muscles is involved?
questions.explanation:
The scenario is unilateral vocal-cord palsy due to involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The posterior cricoarytenoid, marked 3, is paralyzed; it is the abductor of the vocal cord.

In the source figure: 1 is lateral cricoarytenoid, which closes the ligamentous part of the rima glottidis; 2 is transverse arytenoid, which closes the intercartilaginous part; 3 is posterior cricoarytenoid; and 4 is cricothyroid, the tensor of the vocal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about the sensory innervation of the larynx?

options.text: Above the level of vocal cords - Superior laryngeal nerve
Above the level of vocal cords - Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Below the level of vocal cords - Internal laryngeal nerve
Below the level of vocal cords - External laryngeal nerve

questions.correctAnswerText: Above the level of vocal cords - Superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation:
Sensory innervation above the level of the vocal cords is through the internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Below the vocal cords it is through the recurrent laryngeal nerve. At the level of the cords, both internal and recurrent laryngeal nerves contribute.

All intrinsic muscles of the larynx are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which among the following is false about larynx?

options.text: External laryngeal nerve supplies all larynx muscles except cricothyroid
Cricothyroid is a tensor of vocal cord

questions.correctAnswerText: External laryngeal nerve supplies all larynx muscles except cricothyroid
questions.explanation:
The false statement is that the external laryngeal nerve supplies all laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid. In fact, the external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

The larynx contains three paired cartilages (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform) and three unpaired cartilages (epiglottis, thyroid, cricoid). Triticeal cartilage may also be present as a variable small cartilage within the lateral thyrohyoid membrane.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: While performing total thyroidectomy, a nerve coursing along the superior thyroid artery is injured. Which of the following is a probable consequence?

options.text: Loss of sensation above the vocal cords
Loss of sensation below the vocal cords

questions.explanation:
The nerve closely related to the superior thyroid artery is the external laryngeal nerve. Injury causes paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle, the principal tensor of the vocal cord, leading to decreased pitch of voice.

The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane at a higher level and is therefore not the nerve described. Other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.explanation: Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve causes vocal-cord paralysis because it supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid. Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A chronic smoker presented with a supraglottic growth, which was later found to be squamous cell carcinoma. How will this spread to the pre-epiglottic space?
questions.explanation:
Supraglottic tumors can spread to the pre-epiglottic space through multiple perforations in the epiglottic cartilage.

The pre-epiglottic space lies anterior to the epiglottis. Its superior relation is the hyoepiglottic membrane/median hyoepiglottic ligament; inferior relation is the thyroepiglottic ligament; anterior relations are the thyrohyoid membrane and median thyrohyoid ligament; posterior relation is the epiglottis; laterally it is related to the greater cornua of the hyoid superiorly and is continuous with the paraglottic space inferiorly.

The paraglottic space contains the laryngeal nerve and is continuous superiorly with the pre-epiglottic space; its inferior relation is the cricothyroid joint, posterior relation the piriform fossa, lateral relation the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane, and medial relation the quadrangular membrane above and conus elasticus below.
questions.structuredExplanationText:
Supraglottic tumors can spread to the pre-epiglottic space through multiple perforations in the epiglottic cartilage.

The pre-epiglottic space lies anterior to the epiglottis. Its superior relation is the hyoepiglottic membrane/median hyoepiglottic ligament; inferior relation is the thyroepiglottic ligament; anterior relations are the thyrohyoid membrane and median thyrohyoid ligament; posterior relation is the epiglottis; laterally it is related to the greater cornua of the hyoid superiorly and is continuous with the paraglottic space inferiorly.

The paraglottic space contains the laryngeal nerve and is continuous superiorly with the pre-epiglottic space; its inferior relation is the cricothyroid joint, posterior relation the piriform fossa, lateral relation the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane, and medial relation the quadrangular membrane above and conus elasticus below.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: All of the following statements are true except:

options.text: Vagus nerve emerges via the intermediate compartment of jugular foramen
Galen's anastomosis refers to anastomosis between the internal laryngeal nerve and recurrent laryngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve is accompanied by superior thyroid vessels
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve winds around the 1st part of subclavian artery

questions.correctAnswerText: Internal laryngeal nerve is accompanied by superior thyroid vessels
questions.explanation:
The false statement is that the internal laryngeal nerve is accompanied by the superior thyroid vessels. It is accompanied by the superior laryngeal vessels and, together with them, pierces the thyrohyoid membrane.

The vagus nerve emerges through the intermediate compartment of the jugular foramen. Galen's anastomosis is a communicating branch between the inferior laryngeal nerve (from the recurrent laryngeal nerve) and the internal laryngeal nerve (from the superior laryngeal nerve). The right recurrent laryngeal nerve winds around the lower/posterior aspect of the first part of the right subclavian artery, while the left recurrent laryngeal nerve winds around the aortic arch.
